headline: The Problems, Services & Recovery Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet clerks and officials, give numbers, times and prices, say what is lost, stolen or blocked, ask where, when and how much, make polite requests, and start Problems, Services & Recovery Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet clerks and officials politely and pronounce key travel words like pasaporte, llave and embajada.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent, plus greetings with clerks

words.note: Pure, short vowels: pa-sa-POR-te. Every e sounds like 'eh'.
In Mexico, la cartera is a wallet. Stress: car-TE-ra.
Usual word for a phone in Mexico. Stress on the last syllable: ce-lu-LAR.
ch sounds like the ch in 'church'.
j is a breathy h sound: em-ba-HA-da.
In most of Mexico, ll sounds like English y: YA-ve.
rr is a rolled, trilled r. Carro is the usual word for car in Mexico.
An r at the start of a word is rolled like rr.
The written accent marks the stress: po-li-CÍ-a.
ñ sounds like the ny in 'canyon'.
Debit or credit card. j is a breathy h: tar-HE-ta.
Use buenos días until about noon.

words.en: Good afternoon, my name is Sam.
words.note: Buenas tardes from noon until dark; buenas noches after dark.
Formal. Use usted with clerks, officers and bank staff.

lessons.speaking: Greet a hotel receptionist, say your name, and say three travel words aloud, such as pasaporte, llave and celular.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say prices in pesos, clock times, days, blocks and kilos of laundry while you sort out a problem.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, and pesos, days, nights, blocks and kilos of laundry

words.note: Mexican money. Prices are said as a number plus pesos: 200 pesos.
Laundromats in Mexico often charge for laundry by the kilo.
Masculine even though it ends in -a: el día.
A city block. A 3 cuadras = 3 blocks away.
Common word for a hotel room in Mexico.
Use son las for hours; es la only for 1: es la 1.

lessons.speaking: Tell a laundromat attendant how many kilos of clothes you have, your room number, and what time your flight leaves.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who you are and where you are from, and describe things as lost, stolen, blocked, open or closed.
lessons.focus: ser for identity and origin, estar for condition or location (blocked, lost, closed)

words.note: Agrees with the thing: el celular perdido, la cartera perdida.
Agrees: el pasaporte robado, la mochila robada.
Banks say la tarjeta está bloqueada.
For objects: el celular está roto.
A woman says estoy nerviosa.
ser: where you are from.
ser for who you are. No article after soy.
estar: a condition that can change.
estar for location.

lessons.speaking: Tell a hotel clerk where you are from, say that your card is blocked, and ask whether the laundromat is open or closed.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what you have, need and want, ask if there is an ATM, and say what has to be done.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive

words.note: In Mexico a SIM card is usually called el chip.
Mobile data: un plan de datos.
Common for a police or incident report; officials may say la denuncia.
Pagar en efectivo = pay in cash.
Often just el cajero.
Singular in Spanish: la ropa está sucia.

words.en: I have a copy of my passport.
words.es: Tengo una copia de mi pasaporte.

words.note: Hay = there is / there are; it never changes.

words.en: I need a SIM card for my phone.
words.es: Necesito un chip para mi celular.

words.en: We have to call the bank.
words.note: Hay que + infinitive: it is necessary to. a + el = al.

lessons.speaking: Tell a phone-shop worker what you have, what you need and want for your phone, and ask if there is an ATM nearby.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say where you are going, what you plan to do, and what you can do to fix a travel problem.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer, and poder

words.note: Offices often ask you to hacer una cita (make an appointment).
La mañana means the morning; mañana alone means tomorrow.

words.en: I'm going to the police station.
words.es: Voy a la estación de policía.

words.en: I'm going to change my flight tomorrow.
words.es: Voy a cambiar mi vuelo mañana.
words.note: ir a + infinitive for plans.

words.en: Can I make an appointment for today?
I can pay for the taxi in cash.
words.es: Puedo pagar el taxi en efectivo.

words.note: Hago is the yo form of hacer.

lessons.speaking: Tell a hotel clerk where you are going today and what you are going to do tomorrow, and ask if you can make an appointment.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Use everyday present-tense verbs to talk about laundry, tickets, payments and your trip.
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs for yo, tú, usted, nosotros, ellos

words.note: Jabón is soap; at a laundromat it means laundry detergent.
In Mexico a bus or plane ticket is el boleto.
yo form: -ar verbs end in -o.

words.en: Do you sell SIM cards here?
words.note: usted form of -er verbs ends in -e.
nosotros form of -ir verbs ends in -imos.

words.en: Do you take cards or only cash?
words.note: ellos / ustedes form: -ar verbs end in -an.

words.en: You pay for the taxi and I pay for dinner.
words.es: Tú pagas el taxi y yo pago la cena.
words.note: Informal tú, for a travel companion or friend.

lessons.speaking: Ask a shop worker if they sell SIM cards and accept cards, then tell your travel companion who pays for what.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask the basic questions you need at a police desk, embassy, bank or phone shop.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: ¿Cuántos? / ¿Cuántas? for how many: ¿cuántas noches?
¿Cómo? alone also means 'pardon?' when you didn't hear.
Two words for why; porque (one word) means because.
Use cuál before es: ¿Cuál es su nombre?

words.en: How much does the SIM card cost?
What do I need for the report?
How do I get to the police station?
words.es: ¿Cómo llego a la estación de policía?

lessons.speaking: Ask an embassy worker where the office is, when it opens, what you need, and who can help you.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say no, never and not yet, refuse a pushy offer, and ask for more, less or another one.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no before the verb; más, menos and otro for amounts

words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: no quiero nada.
Never put un before it: otro chip, otra copia.
Mexican banks say NIP. Never say yours aloud or give it to anyone.

words.en: I never give my PIN over the phone.
words.es: Nunca doy mi NIP por teléfono.

words.note: Personal a before nadie when it is the person you know.

words.en: I don't have the report yet.

words.note: A firm, polite way to leave a pushy sale.

words.en: It's a lot, I don't want to pay more.
words.es: Es mucho, no quiero pagar más.

lessons.speaking: Politely turn down a pushy street seller, then tell a bank agent you never give your PIN over the phone.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Make polite requests at an office window and give simple usted commands when you need help.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede + infinitive? for polite requests and usted commands (hable, escriba, llame, espere)

words.note: The counter window at a bank, office or station.
Hacer fila = to wait in line.
Many forms ask for two apellidos; write yours as it appears on your passport.
Also means direction.

words.en: Can you speak more slowly, please?
words.note: ¿Puede...? is polite with usted.

words.en: Can you give me a copy of the report?
words.es: ¿Me puede dar una copia del reporte?
Escriba la dirección aquí, por favor.
words.note: usted command: -ar verbs end in -e, -er/-ir verbs in -a.

words.es: Llame a la policía, por favor.

lessons.speaking: Ask a police clerk to speak more slowly, to write the address down, and to give you a copy of the report.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize cognates like información and emergencia and use survival phrases to get help fast.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, plus survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
Common in Mexico; Spain says la reserva.
-dad words are feminine and match English -ty.
-ente often matches English -ent.
A woman is la agente.
Formal usted form, right for officials and clerks.

words.en: I have a reservation under my name.
words.es: Tengo una reservación a mi nombre.

lessons.speaking: Tell a public-service employee you don't understand, ask if they speak English, and say that it is an emergency.
